topic: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): From Chaos to Order

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions
sections.content: Briefly review that a 'distribution' shows how often values occur. Contrast a 'Normal Distribution' (bell curve) with 'Non-normal Distributions' (uniform, skewed, or irregular shapes).
sections.example: Visual: A set of six-sided dice showing a uniform distribution vs. a slanted graph representing biased coin flips.

sections.title: The Problem: Does the Parent Distribution Matter?
sections.content: Pose the question: What happens if we take a random sample from a weird, non-normal population and calculate the mean? Does the average of those samples look like the original population?
sections.example: Visual: An animation of 'Professor Squirrel' picking random nuts from a pile of various sizes (skewed distribution) and logging their average weight.

sections.title: The Experiment: Building the Sampling Distribution
sections.content: Explain the process: Take many samples of size 'n', calculate the mean for each, and plot these means on a new graph. As 'n' increases, watch the shape change.
sections.example: Visual: Fast-forward animation of 1,000 squirrels picking groups of 30 nuts. As the bars fill the graph, they start forming a perfect bell-shaped curve despite the original nut sizes being all over the place.

sections.title: The Core Revelation: The Central Limit Theorem
sections.content: Formally define the CLT: No matter the shape of the original population, the distribution of sample means will approach a Normal Distribution as the sample size increases (typically n ≥ 30).
sections.example: Visual: An overlay of a 'Chaotic Cloud' of data points transforming into a rigid, symmetric 'Bell Curve' as the 'Sample Size' slider moves from 1 to 30.

sections.title: Why It Matters: Real-World Application
sections.content: Explain that CLT is the foundation of inferential statistics. It allows us to make predictions about a population using only a small, manageable sample.
sections.example: Visual: A smartphone app calculating 'average battery life' for millions of devices based on testing just 30 units, represented by a clear confidence interval bar popping up on screen.
